kurz: How the Black-Scholes formula calculates an option price from six inputs and what five metrics say about how a position will behave from here on.

bloecke.md:
Until 1973, options were traded without anyone being able to say what they were worth. In that year, Fischer Black and Myron Scholes supplied the argument that closed this gap, and Robert Merton, working in parallel, a more general form of it. The argument is based on arbitrage and contains no forecast. With the underlying and a loan in a continuously adjusted ratio, the payoff of an option can be replicated exactly. If the option costs more than this replicating portfolio, you sell it and replicate it. If it costs less, the trade runs the other way. Because a risk-free profit does not persist, the option price must equal the price of the replica.

The expected return of the underlying therefore does not appear in the formula, which is surprising at first. Whether the share is considered undervalued plays no role in the option price; only its fluctuation counts. In 1997, Scholes and Merton received the Nobel Prize in Economics; Black had died in 1995.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula applies to European options on an underlying with a continuous dividend yield q. Without a dividend (q = 0), the factor e^(-q×T) drops out. N(x) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. It cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions and is evaluated numerically.

Volatility p.a., standard deviation of returns

bloecke.md:
Five of the six inputs can be read off: price, strike, remaining term, interest rate and dividend yield. The sixth, volatility, cannot be read off, because nobody knows how much the price will fluctuate over the coming three months. In practice, the formula is therefore used backwards. You enter the observed market price and search numerically for the σ that reproduces it. This σ is called [[implied volatility]].

Black-Scholes thus serves above all to convert option prices into volatilities. A premium of €5.29 says nothing on its own. The statement “the market is pricing in 25% annual volatility”, on the other hand, can be compared across strikes, maturities and underlyings. Traders therefore quote options in volatility points rather than in euros.

The share is at €100, and the call has a strike of 100 and a remaining term of three months (T = 0.25). The risk-free rate is 2.5% p.a. and is therefore of the same order of magnitude as the ECB deposit facility rate, which has stood at 2.50% since 16 September 2026. No dividend is paid during the term, and implied volatility is 25%.

- σ × √T = 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.125, the expected fluctuation over the term (12.5% of the price)
- d1 = [ln(1) + (0.025 + 0.03125) × 0.25] / 0.125 = 0.01406 / 0.125 = 0.1125
- d2 = 0.1125 - 0.125 = -0.0125
- N(d1) = 0.5448; N(d2) = 0.4950; e^(-0.025 × 0.25) = 0.99377
- C = 100 × 0.5448 - 100 × 0.99377 × 0.4950 = 54.48 - 49.19 = €5.29
- P = 100 × 0.99377 × 0.5050 - 100 × 0.4552 = 50.18 - 45.52 = €4.66

Put-call parity serves as a check: C - P = 5.29 - 4.66 = 0.63 and S - K × e^(-r×T) = 100 - 99.38 = 0.62. The difference of one cent comes from rounding; with unrounded prices, both sides come to 0.623. The two prices are therefore consistent. With the usual contract size of 100 shares, this call costs €529. Forgetting the multiplier is the most common calculation error made by beginners.

For an at-the-money option, the approximation premium ≈ 0.4 × S × σ × √T applies. In the example, it gives 0.4 × 100 × 0.25 × 0.5 = €5.00 compared with exactly €5.29. This allows you to check any quoted premium for plausibility in seconds, and conversely to estimate implied volatility. The approximation comes from the series expansion of the formula at the money and becomes inaccurate with very long terms or high interest rates.

Black-Scholes assumes constant volatility, a constant interest rate, no jumps, lognormally distributed returns, infinitely divisible units and continuous, cost-free re-hedging. None of these assumptions holds in reality. Real returns have fat tails and negative skewness. Extreme days therefore occur much more often than a normal distribution allows.

Market prices take this into account. Since the 1987 crash, out-of-the-money index puts have systematically had a higher implied volatility than calls a comparable distance away. This difference is called the volatility skew. With a single σ for all strikes, the model therefore gets it wrong precisely where the losses arise. The collapse of the hedge fund LTCM in 1998, whose partners included Merton and Scholes, showed that even the inventors themselves were not protected against such errors.

## The Greeks

The price alone says nothing about how the position will behave tomorrow. This is what the partial derivatives of the formula, named after Greek letters, are for. They are local measures, which means they describe the reaction to a small change and become inaccurate when prices jump.

The conventions for stating them are largely standard and important, because the pure derivatives would have different units: [[vega]] is stated per volatility point, [[theta]] per calendar day and rho per percentage point change in interest rates.

bloecke.titel: The five metrics at a glance
zeilen: Price change per €1 move in the underlying
Change in delta per €1 move in the underlying

bloecke.titel: Three strikes on the same share, illustrative calculation (S = 100, T = 0.25, r = 2.5%, σ = 25%)

bloecke.md:
Three relationships can be read from the table. First, delta rises with moneyness from 0.26 to 0.83, so the deep in-the-money option behaves almost like the share itself. Second, [[gamma]] and vega are greatest at the money. That is where the outcome is most open, so the price reacts most strongly to price movements and to changes in volatility. Third, time decay is highest at the money, because that is where there is the most time value to lose.

Delta can be read in three ways. As a sensitivity, it states that the at-the-money call gains around 54 cents for each euro the price rises. As a hedge ratio, a delta of 0.5448 means that a sold contract on 100 shares is largely neutralised by 54 shares bought. Finally, delta can be read as a rough probability that the option will expire in the money. Caution is needed here, because the model probability for this is N(d2), 0.495 in the example compared with a delta of 0.545. The difference grows with the term and with volatility. N(d2) is also a risk-neutral quantity and says nothing about the real world.

bloecke.titel: Delta of a call at two remaining terms
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with K = 100, r = 0, q = 0, σ = 20%. The closer expiry comes, the steeper the S-curve becomes, until it almost resembles a step at the strike price.

bloecke.md: The slope of this curve is gamma, and it increases sharply at the money as expiry approaches. Shortly before expiry, a few points of price movement decide whether the option expires worthless or ends in the money, and delta jumps from almost 0 to almost 1. For the option writer, the last week is therefore the most dangerous. The writer's gamma is most strongly negative there, so every price movement works against them, whichever way they re-hedge.

The call from the example is at €5.29, with a delta of 0.545 and a gamma of 0.0317.

The share rises by €5 to 105.
- Estimate using delta only: 5.29 + 0.545 × 5 = €8.01
- With gamma correction (+ ½ × gamma × price change²): 8.01 + 0.5 × 0.0317 × 25 = €8.41
- Exact value using Black-Scholes: €8.39

The share falls by €10 to 90.
- Estimate using delta only: 5.29 - 0.545 × 10 = -€0.16, that is, a negative option price, which cannot exist
- With gamma correction: -0.16 + 0.5 × 0.0317 × 100 = €1.42
- Exact value: €1.44

Delta describes a tangent to the price curve. Over five points this approximation is usable; over ten points it no longer is. A position that is hedged using delta and not readjusted afterwards is wrongly positioned after every larger move. For sellers of options, this always works to their disadvantage.

bloecke.titel: Time value of an at-the-money option over the remaining term
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a call with S = K = 100, r = 2.5% and σ = 25%. The value roughly follows the square root of the remaining term. With 180 days remaining, it is only around 32% lower than with 365 days; under the pure square-root rule, it would be around 30%. The difference is due to the 2.5% interest rate. In the last quarter, by contrast, the value falls steeply to zero.

serien.name: Option value in euros per share

bloecke.titel: Daily time decay (theta) of the same option
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation, theta in cents per share and calendar day at the respective remaining term. One day before expiry, it is just under sixteen times the value one year before expiry; over the last day, the entire remaining value of 53 cents is lost.

bloecke.md:
Per contract, the at-the-money call with three months to expiry loses around €3 a day, and around €10 a day one week before expiry. On the last day, the entire remaining value of around €53 is lost. This time decay explains why cheap, short-dated out-of-the-money options expire worthless so reliably. The reason is not that the direction is usually misjudged. Time value inevitably runs towards zero, and towards the end there is less and less time left for this to happen.

The counterpart to time decay is vega. The same option loses or gains €0.198 per share, just under €20 per contract, when implied volatility falls or rises by one point. Option buyers are long gamma and long vega but short theta. Price movements and rising implied volatility earn them money; an unchanged price costs them money. For the option writer, the opposite applies in each case.

bloecke.titel: A loss despite the right direction
bloecke.md:
Before quarterly results, the share is at €100. The call with a strike of 105 and seven days remaining costs €0.80. It contains an implied volatility of 45%, because the market is pricing in the event.

The results are published, and the share rises by 3% to 103. This resolves the uncertainty, and implied volatility falls to 25%.

- With volatility unchanged at 45%, the call would be worth €1.73.
- With volatility down to 25%, it is worth €0.67, a loss of 17%, even though the direction was right.

The loss through vega was greater than the price gain through delta. This IV crush arises neither by chance nor through manipulation. It follows inevitably from the fact that options are more expensive before known events. Investors who use options to bet on quarterly results are therefore betting that the move will be bigger than the one priced in, and not just on the direction.

- The premium is not the measure of risk. Position sizes are based on the maximum loss in a stress scenario.
- Before every purchase, check where implied volatility stands compared with its own history (IV rank). What is meaningful is volatility that is high by historical comparison; a high absolute value alone says nothing.
- Look at theta and vega together. A long term costs less time value per day but reacts much more strongly to changes in volatility.
- Always execute multi-leg positions as a combination order. If the individual parts are traded one after the other, the risk in the meantime is completely different, and the spread is paid twice.
- Add up the Greeks for the entire portfolio instead of looking only at the individual position.

Gains from option transactions are income from capital assets (Einkünfte aus Kapitalvermögen). The gain from a derivative transaction (Termingeschäft) falls under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act), and option writer's premiums received fall under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG. The special tax rate of 25% under Section 32d(1) EStG applies, plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge. Together that comes to 26.375%, or around 27.8% to 28.0% with church tax.

The former limit of €20,000 a year on offsetting losses from derivative transactions was abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 and no longer applies in any open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). The basic rule of Section 20(6) EStG continues to apply. Losses from capital assets can only be offset within capital income, that is, not against employment income or other types of income. Losses that are not offset are carried forward indefinitely. This information does not replace tax advice.

mitnehmen: The Black-Scholes formula predicts nothing; it determines the price at which an option can be replicated from the underlying and a loan, and the expected return of the underlying does not appear in it.
Of the six inputs, only volatility cannot be observed, so the formula is used backwards and provides implied volatility as the common yardstick of the options market.

Delta is a tangent that only applies to small movements, and gamma measures how quickly it becomes unusable; the model probability of expiring in the money is N(d2), and delta indicates it only roughly.
Option buyers are long gamma, long vega and short theta, and their time decay accelerates towards expiry and is greatest at the money.
A slump in implied volatility after an event that was priced in can completely cancel out the price gain, which is why getting the direction right is not enough with options.

begriffe.text: The volatility that, when entered into an option pricing model, exactly reproduces the observed market price. It is forward-looking and is determined numerically, unlike historical volatility, which is derived from past prices.

Change in the option price per unit change in the price of the underlying. Delta lies between 0 and 1 for a call and between -1 and 0 for a put, corresponds to the hedge ratio and gives only a rough indication of the probability of expiring in the money.

Change in delta per unit of price change, that is, the curvature of the price curve. Gamma is greatest at the money and shortly before expiry, and it determines how quickly a delta hedge becomes unusable.
Change in the option price per percentage point of implied volatility. Vega is the same for calls and puts, is greatest at the money and falls as the remaining term shortens.
Change in the option price for each calendar day that passes. Theta is negative for option buyers and positive for option writers; its magnitude increases disproportionately towards expiry.
